## PDF page 180

[Open source PDF](../../../../sources/pdf/GTO/Poker-Math-Preflop-Workbook.pdf#page=180)

```text
                             CHAPTER FIFTEEN



                            3BETTING


A 3bet is the first re-raise preflop and is the cornerstone of aggressive play
before the flop. By applying pressure to your opponent’s raising range in the
right spots, you can contend for pots with monsters and bluff hands alike.

Most players avoid 3betting with anything other than huge hands. However,
with some technical exploration, you will be poised to find spots to make prof-
itable 3bets with weaker hands. If you are able to identify situations where
your opponent is folding too often (in this case, more than 75% of the time),
you can add heaps of extra bluffs into your 3betting strategy.

These exercises will guide you through the technical side of 3betting, including
how often different ranges fold against different 3bet sizes and how your size
impacts the SPR. If you are not familiar with SPR, it stands for Stack-to-Pot-
Ratio. This number acts as a guide for how automatically-committed, or not,
we are on the flop. To learn more about how SPR can be used to inform both
your preflop and flop decisions, visit www.splitsuit.pro/spr.

TOOLS TO USE: Any range software and a calculator will work.

PROCESS: Each page contains a single 3bet scenario. Read the prompt and
then begin by filling in the %-form for your opponent’s opening range and the
two possible continuance ranges.



                                   PA G E 1 8 0
```

## PDF page 181

[Open source PDF](../../../../sources/pdf/GTO/Poker-Math-Preflop-Workbook.pdf#page=181)

```text
                            3BETTING: MAKING 3BETS


Then fill out the table below for each 3bet size. Remember that your oppo-
nent’s folding frequency = 100%-(Continuance Range/Original Range). So if
they originally raised with 20% of hands and would continue with 5% of hands
after you 3bet, 100%-(5%/20%) = 75%. This means you can expect them to fold
75% of the time when you 3bet them.

Since you are exploring multiple 3bet sizes, also calculate what the SPR would
be if your opponent called your 3bet. The formula for SPR is:

                   S PR = E F F E C T I V E S TAC K S I Z E / P O T S I Z E


So if you both start with $1,000 stacks and they open to $30 and you 3bet to
$100 – when your opponent calls the pot is $200 and you both have $900
remaining. $900/$200 = 4.5 SPR.

TAKEAWAYS: Some players will get frustrated that no hole cards are given
in these exercises, but most people get distracted by their cards and miss
the big picture. If you find a spot where a player is folding a ton of the time
when you 3bet (75%+), and the players behind you are folding often too, does
it matter much if you hold A3o or T7s? If you find a spot where your opponent
is folding against 3bets rarely (less than 30%), are you really going to add
many weak hands into your 3bet range?

Also, notice how the SPR gets impacted by slight changes in your 3bet size.
The smaller the SPR will be, especially as it drops under 2.5 SPR, the more you
either a.) want to 3bet strong hands preflop or b.) want a lot of outright folds
when bluff 3betting.

GLGL.




                                         PA G E 1 8 1
```
